4Let it run alone

Hand it off; it runs to the end; you check afterwards.

ⓘ Notes
Background / cloud agents, routines and multi-agent teams: nobody watches, so safety comes from isolation, checkable output, and a person pressing the final button.

Why it’s designed this way: Clear, checkable work does not need you present the whole time; save your time for review and decisions.

Stop 4 of 24 📍 App overview › Using agents › Let it run alone
On this page:

🧒 In plain words first

“Letting it work on its own” is like handing a job to someone and checking it later. Nobody is watching, so three things keep it safe: it works somewhere it cannot break anything; what it hands back can be checked; and the step that cannot be undone (merging, sending, paying) is left for you to press.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Here nobody watches the agent as it works. Safety cannot rely on “you can stop it any time”; it relies on three things:

  1. Isolation: it works in a sandbox, a copy or a branch, away from anything that really matters.
  2. Checkable output: it hands back a PR, a report or a draft instead of acting directly, with a way to Evaluation it (tests, a checklist).
  3. People take the irreversible step: merging, sending, paying are yours to press; see Least privilege and human confirmation.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

A background helper is like someone working in another room: you write the task and hand it over; it changes code and runs tests on a separate online machine, then hands back a “list of changes” (a PR) for you to review. Good for jobs that are clear, checkable and not urgent.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

You write the task and hand it off. It opens an isolated cloud environment: gets a copy of the code, installs dependencies, edits, runs tests, then pushes a new branch and opens a pull request (PR). You can run several at once, even with your computer off.

  • Good for: clear, testable, non-urgent work: fix a known bug, add tests, upgrade a dependency, rename across files.
  • Not for: design work that needs frequent decisions, or work that cannot be checked.
  • How it works: the same Agent loop, with test results instead of you judging each step.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

A routine is like an alarm clock you set: at a set time or when a new email arrives, the helper runs through written instructions by itself. Anything that “goes out” is drafted first and sent only after a person checks it; doing the same thing twice still counts once; and every run is written down.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Nobody has to ask: at a set time (9 am daily) or when something happens (a new email, ticket or commit), it runs a fixed prompt automatically.

Example Illustrative: every weekday at 9:00, read yesterday’s new tickets → sort them and find duplicates → write a summary.

  • Draft first: steps that send something out (reply, close a ticket) only produce a draft until a person approves.
  • Idempotent: running twice on the same item has the effect of once (e.g. check “already handled?” first), so retries and catch-up runs never send twice.
  • Keep logs: record what each run did and which tools it used, and look at them regularly.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Several helpers working together is like a group project: the leader splits the big task, gives each member a piece, and someone checks and combines the results at the end. Working at the same time saves time but costs more; each member’s task must be written out fully, because they cannot hear what the leader and you discussed.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

An Orchestrator splits a big task, sends parts to several Workers, and a Reviewer checks and merges. Each sub-agent has its own clean context and sees only its part.

A rough sum Illustrative: research 3 directions, 4 minutes each. One agent in turn takes 12 minutes; 3 in parallel take about 4, plus 1 to merge. The cost: 3 contexts, so it costs more.

  • Good for: work that splits into independent parts.
  • Key point: give each worker a complete brief (it cannot see the coordinator’s chat), and always merge and check at the end.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Why hand back a “list of changes” instead of changing things directly? Like showing your essay to the teacher before pinning it on the wall: at worst it is simply not used and nothing breaks, and with the changes and test results side by side, checking is much faster than redoing it.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

With nobody watching, the worst risk is a mistake taking effect directly. A PR puts every change in a box that can be reviewed and rejected:

  • the worst case is “do not merge”, and nothing is broken;
  • test results and the diff are right in front of you, and reviewing is much faster than doing it yourself;
  • “merge” changes the main line for good, so a person presses it.

A routine’s “draft first” follows the same logic.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

More hands do not always help. Research found that several helpers working together often coordinate badly; many runs fail, they are often not much better than one helper, and they cost a lot more. Only jobs that split into independent pieces, each needing lots of reading, are worth trying.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Multi-agent sounds stronger, but the research is more sober:

  • The MAST study (UC Berkeley and others) annotated 1642 traces from 7 multi-agent frameworks and found 14 failure modes in 3 groups: system design issues, inter-agent misalignment and task verification. On 7 open-source multi-agent systems, failure rates ran from 41% to 86.7%, and gains over single-agent or best-of-N baselines were often small.
  • An AI lab’s engineering post on its research system says that agents use about 4× the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about 15×, and that tasks where all agents need the same context or have many dependencies (such as most coding) are a poor fit.
Worth tryingThe work splits into independent parts that each need a lot of reading (say, researching several directions); the task is valuable enough to justify the extra tokens.
Not yetSteps depend on each other and share one context; one agent with good prompts and tools can finish it; there is no way to check the result.

If you do, target MAST’s three groups: write clear roles; define when the job counts as done; add an independent Reviewer to check the result at the end. In the MAST authors’ case study, adding a high-level objective check to one open-source framework raised success by 15.6%.

Sources: Cemri et al. 2025 · Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST) · How we built our multi-agent research system · Overseas academic / legal site: access from mainland China not tested, and no verified mainland mirror found

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

“Deep research” is like sending several classmates to the library to look things up: one makes the plan, a few each search one direction, they come back and combine what they found, search again if needed, and finally mark every statement with its source. When you get the report, open a few sources yourself to check the original really says that.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Many AI products have a “deep research” mode: you ask a question and it spends minutes searching and reading on its own, then returns a cited report. Each vendor does it differently; below is one approach an AI lab has published (see sources) (an Orchestrator plus Workers):

  1. PlanThe lead agent works out an approach and saves the plan to memory, so it survives a long context.
  2. Search in parallelIt spawns subagents, one per direction; each starts with broad queries, then narrows.
  3. Read and judgeAfter each batch of results, a subagent thinks: is this enough, is it reliable, what next?
  4. Merge, and loop if neededThe lead merges the findings and decides whether more research is needed; if so, another round goes out.
  5. CiteA dedicated step matches each claim in the report to its source.

The post’s rules of thumb: a simple fact needs 1 agent and 3–10 tool calls; a comparison 2–4 subagents; only complex research uses more than 10. Their human testers also found agents favouring SEO content farms over authoritative sources.

So when the report arrives, spot-check the citations: open a few links and see whether the source really says that, and whether it is a primary source.

Sources: How we built our multi-agent research system

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

A “workflow” is like cooking from a recipe: every step is fixed, it is the same each time, and mistakes are easy to find. An “Agent” is like letting the chef decide: more flexible, but the time and result may differ each time. If the steps can be written down in advance, the recipe is steadier.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…This is advice from an engineering article, not a hard rule; many real systems mix the two.

A widely cited engineering post defines them: a workflow orchestrates the model and tools through predefined code paths; an agent lets the model direct its own process and tool use. Compare the same job both ways:

Task Illustrative: turn each week’s customer feedback into a weekly report.

🛤️ As a workflowThe code always runs: ① export this week’s feedback → ② the model labels each item → ③ the model writes a summary → ④ fill a template. Each step is fixed, every run is the same, and a failure is easy to pin to one step.
🤖 As an agentGive it the goal and tools (feedback store, tickets, search, docs) and let it decide what to look up and for how many rounds. If one feature suddenly draws many complaints, it can dig through the related tickets for the cause. More flexible, but the steps, cost and result can differ every run.

The article’s advice: find the simplest solution first and add complexity only when needed. For well-defined tasks whose steps can be fixed in advance, workflows are more predictable and consistent; agents suit open-ended problems where the number of steps can’t be predicted, at the price of more latency and cost.

Sources: Building effective agents

🧪 One vs a team: how many sub-agents

🧒 In plain words first

Split one research task among 1 to 4 sub-helpers and see which way the time and the tokens used move; tick “depend on each other” and compare again (all numbers are illustrative).

ⓘ Minutes and tokens are made up (Illustrative): 4 research parts, 4 minutes and 20k tokens each; each sub-agent’s brief costs 5k tokens, merging takes 1 minute.

Why it’s built this way:
  • Parallel work saves time, not money: each extra sub-agent adds a brief and a context of its own.
  • When parts depend on each other, each waits for the last, so “parallel” turns into a queue with extra handoffs and conflicts. See Multi-agent teams.

👀 Try this:
  • Go from 1 to 4 and watch which way time and total tokens move
  • Tick “depend on each other”, then compare 1 and 4

🧪 Build a routine: simulate a week

🧒 In plain words first

Build a routine and simulate a week: choose when it starts, what it does, and whether it acts directly or drafts first, then see what happens on the day of the hidden “trap” (the events are illustrative).

ⓘ The events are made up (Illustrative); each trigger hides one “trap”.

Why it’s built this way:
  • Actions that only tell you (a digest) are safe to automate; actions that reach other people (reply, close) cannot be taken back once wrong.
  • “Draft first” leaves the irreversible step to a person: slower, but you catch the trap.

    👀 Try this:
    • Pick “Reply to the sender” and switch between the modes; see what happens on the trap day
    • Switch to “Send me a digest”: why does nothing wait for you now?
